title: Autonomous-System-Wide Unique BGP Identifier for BGP-4
summary: This standards-track document relaxes the BGP Identifier definition to a 4-octet unsigned non-zero integer and requires uniqueness only within an autonomous system. It does not change other BGP behavior.

plainLanguage.summary: This update relaxes the BGP Identifier rules. A supporting speaker can use any nonzero four-octet integer, provided identifiers are unique within the autonomous system.

questions: what is the bgp identifier uniqueness rule
can a bgp identifier be used without ipv4
subtitle: Allows a BGP Identifier to be any nonzero four-octet integer unique within an AS.

tldr.problem: Requiring a BGP Identifier to be an IPv4 host address can fail in environments such as IPv6-only networks.
tldr.mechanism: The identifier becomes a nonzero unsigned four-octet integer that should be unique within an AS, with OPEN error and collision rules updated.
tldr.outcome: The RFC says the revisions introduce no backward compatibility issues and updates RFC 4271.

today: RFC 6286 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 4271. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Moving Beyond an IPv4 Identifier
sections.content:
RFC 4271 defines the BGP Identifier as a valid IPv4 host address assigned to the speaker. Deployed BGP code also requires two speakers to have distinct identifiers to establish a connection.

This can be a problem in environments such as IPv6-only networks. RFC 6286 updates the definition and limits the uniqueness requirement to the autonomous system.
sections.plainLanguage: A BGP speaker may not have an IPv4 address to use as its identifier. The update lets it use a number instead.

sections.title: Identifier and OPEN Rules
sections.content:
The identifier is a four-octet, unsigned, nonzero integer that should be unique within an AS. It is determined at startup and remains the same for the speaker's interfaces and peers.

If an OPEN message contains identifier zero, or repeats the local identifier for an internal peer, the speaker uses the Bad BGP Identifier error subcode.
sections.plainLanguage: The identifier is a nonzero number selected when the speaker starts. Speakers within the same AS should not use the same value.

sections.title: Connection Collisions and Compatibility
sections.content:
If external peers with identical identifiers collide while establishing connections, the connection initiated by the speaker with the larger AS number is kept. A BGP Confederation counts as one AS for this uniqueness rule.

The RFC states that an identifier allocated under RFC 4271 fits the revised definition, and that the revisions introduce no backward compatibility issues. A supporting speaker cannot share an identifier with an external neighbor until that neighbor supports the revisions.
sections.plainLanguage: If two external peers share an identifier during a connection collision, the peer with the larger AS number keeps the connection.

references.text: Rekhter, Y., Ed., Li, T., Ed., and S. Hares, Ed., "A Border Gateway Protocol 4 (BGP-4)", RFC 4271, January 2006.
Vohra, Q. and E. Chen, "BGP Support for Four-octet AS Number Space", RFC 4893, May 2007.
